messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Miguel

Miguel was thirty-seven when he first came to the clinic, though his face carried the weight of someone older. He had been a social ministry worker for twelve years, coordinating community outreach programs for at-risk youth in the city—work that had always felt meaningful to him, a way of channeling his own history of struggle into something redemptive. Three years ago, his marriage to David had ended in violence. What had started as an argument in their apartment one evening escalated when David, drunk and enraged, had pinned Miguel against the bedroom wall, one forearm across his chest, the other hand gripping his throat. Miguel had frozen completely, unable to move or call for help, as David's breath—reeking of whiskey—came hot against his face and David's voice, hoarse and vicious, promised consequences if Miguel ever tried to leave. When David finally released him and stormed out, slamming the bedroom door so hard the frame cracked, Miguel had collapsed onto the bed, gasping, certain he was going to die.

The months that followed were a slow unraveling. Miguel had moved out within a week, but the apartment where it happened—a fifteen-minute walk from his workplace—became a place he could not approach. He found himself taking long detours to avoid the street, and once, when a colleague suggested meeting near that neighborhood for lunch, Miguel had invented an excuse so transparent that his coworker had noticed. More troubling was what had begun to happen in his body. Any unexpected movement in his peripheral vision—a colleague turning quickly, a client standing up abruptly during a session—sent a jolt of pure terror through him, as if the threat were immediate and real. He had started checking the locks on his apartment door and windows obsessively, sometimes five or six times before bed, his hands shaking as he tested each one. At night, he felt unsafe in a way that daylight could not quite dispel; even with every lock secured, he would lie awake listening to the building settle, every creak a potential footstep, every distant siren a warning.

When memories of that evening surfaced—and they did, unbidden and vivid—Miguel would hear David's voice again, not as a distant recollection but as an immediate auditory presence in his mind, the slurred words and the ragged breathing replaying with such clarity that he would have to grip the edge of his desk to orient himself to the present. The memory itself was crystalline in a way that felt almost photographic; he could see the exact angle of the afternoon light through the bedroom window, the pattern of the bedspread beneath his hands, the specific shade of rage in David's eyes. Alongside these images came a wave of grief so overwhelming that it would leave him hollow for hours afterward—not grief for the relationship, but grief for the person he had been before that moment, the version of himself who had felt safe in his own home, who had trusted his own judgment about people.

The triggers had become invisible architects of his daily life. The smell of alcohol—on a client's breath, wafting from a bar he passed—would send him spiraling into that bedroom instantly, his body responding as if the threat were current rather than past. When he encountered these smells, his startle response would escalate; his hypervigilance would spike, and he would find himself checking doors again that night, his hands moving automatically through the ritual. The sound of a door opening or closing anywhere in his apartment building would jolt him awake or pull him from concentration, his nervous system interpreting every such sound as a harbinger of danger. Feeling physically restrained in any way—a client standing too close, someone brushing against him on the bus—triggered an immediate urge to freeze, the same paralysis that had seized him during the assault, as if his body remembered that movement meant worse consequences. This freezing, once it began, would pull the memories forward again; he would find himself back in that bedroom, and the vivid details would compound his sense of present danger, making it harder to distinguish past from present.

Over time, Miguel had developed a pattern of emotional control that felt necessary but was slowly suffocating him. He had learned to suppress any visible reaction to his triggers, to keep his face neutral and his breathing steady, terrified that showing fear would invite further harm or mark him as weak. Yet this suppression—the constant effort of not letting anything show, of holding the fear down—seemed to keep the memories themselves fresh and unprocessed; by refusing to speak about that night or to acknowledge what had happened to him, he had left the memory untouched and vivid in his mind, replaying with the same intensity it had held three years ago. Yet this very suppression seemed to deepen the grip of the memories; the effort of holding everything in left him more vulnerable to intrusive recollections, and the memories, in turn, reinforced his conviction that he needed to control every aspect of his emotional presentation. His work had begun to suffer. He had stopped attending evening community events, citing scheduling conflicts, when in truth the thought of being in unfamiliar spaces after dark, where he could not control the exits or predict who might arrive, felt unbearable. His supervisor had asked twice if everything was all right. Miguel had said yes both times, and then had gone home and checked his locks seven times.

It was his therapist at the community health center—a colleague who had gently asked why Miguel had missed the annual staff dinner—who finally named what Miguel had been too ashamed to say aloud: that he was living in a kind of siege, that the trauma was still occupying his body and his home, and that the very strategies he had adopted to protect himself were keeping him trapped in the cycle. Miguel had come to believe that vigilance was the only thing standing between him and catastrophe, that his frozen response had saved his life by preventing David from escalating further, that controlling his emotions was the price of survival. What he had not yet been able to see was that these beliefs, born in a moment of genuine terror, were now the bars of his own prison.
